title: How to Stop Your Puppy From Jumping on People
description: Four paws on the floor earns the attention, so here is how to greet guests calmly and stop the jump before it starts.
excerpt: Four paws on the floor earns the attention, so here is how to greet guests calmly and stop the jump before it starts.
seoTitle: How to Stop Your Puppy From Jumping on People

quick: Stop puppy jumping by rewarding four paws on the floor and turning away or staying still when he jumps. Use a gate or a lead to manage the doorway, ask guests to wait for a sit before petting, and avoid pushing or using your knee. Most puppies improve within a few weeks of consistent greetings, though every puppy is different.

faq.q: Why does my puppy jump on people?
faq.a: Puppies usually jump because it gets results. A jump brings faces close, hands to pet and voices up, so the behavior is rewarded even by a laugh or a sharp word. Excitement, boredom and a natural urge to greet people face to face all play a part. Teaching him that four paws on the floor earns more attention is the most reliable fix.

faq.q: Will my puppy grow out of jumping on people?
faq.a: Some puppies calm down as they mature, but waiting rarely works on its own. A jump that keeps getting rewarded tends to become a stronger habit as the puppy gets bigger and heavier. Teaching a calm greeting now is far easier than changing a strong adult dog's jump later. Every puppy is different, so keep practicing consistently and be patient.

faq.q: Should I push my puppy off when he jumps?
faq.a: No. Pushing, kneeing or pulling a puppy off can turn the greeting into a game, make him more excited, and damage trust. Instead, turn your body away, stay still and wait for four paws on the floor. Then give calm attention and a treat. Consistency from everyone in the household helps the lesson stick.

faq.q: How long does it take to stop puppy jumping up?
faq.a: Many families notice a difference within a few weeks of consistent greetings, but full reliability can take months. Excitable puppies and busy homes with lots of visitors often need longer. Practice with the same people, keep greetings short and reward calm behavior every time. If progress stalls or the jumping gets worse, talk to your veterinarian or a reward-based trainer.

faq.q: How do I stop my puppy jumping on my children?
faq.a: Children are at about face height for a puppy, so jumping can feel startling for them. Teach kids to stand still like a tree, then sit on the floor so the puppy has a low, friendly place to visit. They can offer a treat only when paws are down. Supervise every interaction, and give your puppy a break when he gets too wound up.

faq.q: Is it okay to ignore my puppy when he jumps?
faq.a: Ignoring can work well, as long as you stay still and withhold attention while his feet are off the floor. Turning away is usually more effective than shouting, which can still be rewarding. The key is to pay attention the moment he settles. Ignoring alone can slow the lesson down, so pair it with rewards for calm behavior.

html:
It is 6:30 on a Saturday and your new puppy has just met your sister at the front door. She is wearing a clean white coat, and before anyone has said hello, he has both front paws on her chest. If you have been trying to figure out how to stop puppy from jumping on people, you are in good company. It is one of the most common worries for first-time puppy parents, and the fix is less about discipline than about teaching him where the good stuff happens.

Here is the short answer. Puppies jump because jumping works. It brings faces close, hands to pet and voices up. So stop paying for the jump, pay for four paws on the floor instead, and set up your home so jumping is hard to practice while he is learning. Most puppies start to get it within a few weeks of consistent greetings. Every puppy is different, though, and an excitable pup in a busy house with lots of visitors may take longer.

Why your puppy jumps in the first place

Think about it from his point of view. Your puppy's face sits low, and people's faces are high. When a visitor bends down, talks in a bright voice and reaches out, a puppy hears a clear invitation: come up here. Jumping is simply a friendly hello that happens to be too big for a small dog with sharp claws.

Excitement plays a part too. A puppy who has spent two hours in his crate, or who has just survived an afternoon with a noisy toddler, can be wound up enough that jumping is the only outlet he can find. Many puppies also lick faces when they jump, which mirrors the way young dogs greet adults. Whatever the reason, the jump keeps coming back whenever someone reacts, even if that reaction is only a laugh or a sharp word. Attention of any kind counts as a reward in a puppy's mind.

Four paws on the floor gets the attention

The core idea is simple. Pay for four paws, and quietly withdraw your attention from anything else. When your puppy is standing or sitting with all feet on the ground, give him what he wants: a soft word, a pat, a treat. When his feet leave the floor, the fun pauses.

Timing matters more than anything else here. Your attention has to arrive while his paws are down, not a second after he has launched. Keep a small pouch of soft treats by the front door and near the sofa where people usually sit. Picture a lively puppy who jumps on everyone in the first week and then, a few weeks later, offers a sit at the gate before anyone has even reached for him. That shift happens when calm gets rewarded again and again. It won't look the same for every puppy, so judge progress by how often he chooses four paws, not by a date on the calendar.

Manage the doorway before the greeting

Management means arranging things so the jump rarely happens while you are teaching the new skill. Think of it as taking the practice reps out for now. A baby gate, a closed door, a playpen or a loose lead clipped to a harness all help. If your puppy is already settling into a crate, a chew in there during a delivery driver's visit gives him something calm to do. Our guide to crate training a puppy covers how to build that habit gently.

Management alone won't teach him much. A puppy behind a gate will still want to launch the second it opens. Use management to buy yourself time, and use the greeting routine below to teach him what to do with that time.

A calm greeting, step by step

Guests can help a lot, and most people are happy to join in once they know what to do. Try this routine each time someone arrives.

  1. Before the door opens, put your puppy on a lead, behind a gate, or in another room for a minute to settle.
  2. Ask your visitor to come in and stand still with relaxed arms, without bending over or making a big fuss.
  3. Bring your puppy in on a loose lead and ask for a sit, using a treat lure if he needs help.
  4. The moment all four paws are on the floor, your visitor offers a calm pet and a treat is delivered.
  5. If he jumps, your visitor turns their body sideways and waits, with no eye contact and no words. When he settles, the greeting starts again.
  6. Keep it short. End the greeting while he is still happy, then give him a chew or toy in a separate spot.

Repeat this many times across the first few weeks, ideally with the same few people. Variety comes later. Early on, consistency teaches faster than anything else, so it helps if everyone in the house is doing the same thing.

Visitors, children and the hallway

Puppy jumping on guests is the situation most owners want to fix first, and it is also where the stakes feel highest. A friend holding a hot drink or a grandparent with a fragile hip does not want a growing puppy launching at them. Before people arrive, tell them the plan and ask them to wait for a sit. If a visitor would rather not take part, ask them to ignore him and stand still. That alone helps a lot.

Children need a slightly different plan. At child height, a puppy's jump can be startling for kids and sometimes for the puppy too. Teach children to stand still like a tree, and once the puppy is calm, to sit on the floor so he has a low, friendly place to visit. They can offer a treat only when paws are down. Supervise every interaction, and give your puppy a break when he gets too wound up. The same rules work at home, too. Everyone who comes through the door, including you after a long day at work, should follow the same four paws rule, so the message stays consistent.

Why pushing and knee-blocking backfire

Many people reach for a knee, a hand against the chest or a firm shove the moment a puppy jumps. It feels quick, and it is understandable. But for a puppy, being pushed can look a lot like a game. Physical reactions often turn a jump into a tug, a mouthing session or a more excited second round. Some pups learn that greetings get bigger rather than smaller. Keep your hands and knees to yourself, keep your feet still, and let calm turning away and rewarding do the work.

Shouting has the same problem. A loud voice is still attention, and many puppies find it rewarding in its own way. If jumping turns into nipping at hands, the two lessons overlap, so our article on how to stop puppy biting is a useful next read.

How long this takes, by age

Every puppy is different. Breed, temperament, how many visitors you have, and how consistent everyone is will all change the timing. Treat this table as a rough picture rather than a schedule you must hit.

AgeWhat you might seeWhat to focus on
8 to 10 weeksLots of enthusiasm, frequent jumping, short attention spanShort greetings, treats for four paws, a managed doorway
10 to 12 weeksStarts testing rules with new peopleSame routine, add a clear sit cue, practice with the same few visitors
3 to 4 monthsBigger, faster and more confidentLead or gate for guests, reward calm arrivals, consistent household rules
4 to 6 monthsAdolescent wobbles and some setbacksStay patient, go back to basics if jumping returns, practice in different rooms

8 to 10 weeks

At this stage your puppy is still learning how people work and how his own body works. Jumping is often more about excitement than defiance. Keep greetings brief, expect mistakes, and reward every bit of calm you see. The first days and nights home are a big adjustment, so do not expect perfection yet. For that early settling period, our first night at home guide walks through what tends to help.

10 to 12 weeks

Many puppies start testing boundaries around this age. A jump that was rare last week might suddenly happen every time the doorbell rings. This is a normal wobble, not a failure. Go back to the step-by-step greeting, shorten the visits if needed, and make sure every person who greets him is doing the same thing.

3 to 4 months

Your puppy is faster and stronger now, so the same jump lands harder. This is when management pays off most. A lead, a gate or a sit-before-visitors rule keeps the behavior from getting rehearsed while you keep teaching the replacement. Expect some guests to need a friendly reminder, too.

4 to 6 months

Some puppies go through an adolescent phase where old habits resurface, especially when they are very excited or in a new place. If that happens, don't panic. Return to the basics in a quiet room, reward four paws generously, and then build back up to busier spaces and new people.

When to ask a professional

Most jumping is a training issue, not a medical one. Still, talk to your veterinarian if your puppy seems to hurt, limps, or yelps after jumping, or if he is unusually stiff or unwilling to move. Also reach out if the jumping comes with snapping, growling, or fear that doesn't ease with time. A vet can check that nothing physical is driving the behavior, and a reward-based trainer can help you tailor the plan to your puppy and your household. Please don't wait if something worries you.
